transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Start: 09:32 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording ID: zoom.us/rec/abc123 (redacted)
Attendees: Evan Brooks (Redwood AE), Sofia Nguyen (Redwood SE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SRE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SA); Rajiv Menon (Nimbus Head ML Infra), Claire Dubois (Platform Eng), Marco Silva (CTO), Hannah Lee (Security), Jamal Peters (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive on multi-region edge proxy routing, fallback policies, and KV cache warmup strategies for Nimbus Health's hybrid environment (VPC + on-prem).
- Discussed sticky session tradeoffs, cold-start vs. pre-warm KV cache approaches, quantization fallbacks for reduced capacity, and private peering constraints.
- Agreed action items: share capacity spreadsheet, run KV warmup demo, draft failover playbook, schedule DR tabletop.

Topics: edge proxy routing, region capacity, KV cache warmup, batching impact on latency, quantization fallback, VPC peering, DR runbook

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Evan: hey everybody, thanks for joining. i, uh, i see most of the team on board. quick check — audio ok?
[00:00:12] Rajiv: yep can hear you, loud and clear.
[00:00:16] Evan: awesome. quick agenda: one, run through how our edge proxy decides region routing and fallback policies, two, kv-warmup and cache-coherency options, three, quantization and batching fallbacks for regional capacity shortfalls, and four, DR/runbook steps. Sofia will take most of the technical deep dive.
[00:00:34] Sofia: hey. so high-level first — we assume Nimbus will use a mix of hosted Redwood regions plus your private VPC peered cluster in eu-west-2, right? Marco confirmed hybrid?
[00:00:46] Marco: yeah hybrid. primary traffic region is eu-west-2 and we have a smaller us-east-onprem cluster for disaster recovery and some latency-sensitive US users.
[00:00:57] Sofia: got it. so the edge proxy layer we've been proposing sits in front of the routing plane. it can do policy routing by origin IP, cookie/sticky session, and by SLO tag (latency vs cost). default is shortest-latency preference with capacity-aware weighting.
[00:01:15] Claire: quick question — does that weighting use real-time queue depth or just a moving average of observed p99?
[00:01:22] Sofia: we can do both. by default we use a hybrid: immediate instance-level queue depth + 60s rolling p95/p99 for smoothing. the queue depth triggers soft-routing thresholds to avoid oscillation.
[00:01:35] Jamal: when queue depth spikes, do you automatically shift traffic to other regions or go into queued mode in-region?
[00:01:42] Sofia: policy-configurable. you can choose immediate reroute (hard-failover) when a region crosses 85% of committed capacity, or gradual reroute which moves X% of new sessions off-region per minute.
[00:01:55] Rajiv: for compliance, we need sticky sessions inside eu only. cross-region failover is only allowed for DR except for a small set of anonymized endpoints.
[00:02:05] Hannah: yes, security needs geo-fence on PHI endpoints — default routing must respect data residency tags.
[00:02:12] Evan: we'll make sure routing policy has per-route residency tags. next i'll hand to Sofia to sketch the failover sequences — cold-start versus warm pool and how KV cache plays in.
[00:02:24] Sofia: cool. so warm pool approach: maintain a standby pool in each region with minimal instances pre-loaded with model weights and kv cache primed for common prefixes. warm pool size determined by expected burst QPS and startup time.
[00:02:39] Marco: what's typical warm pool overhead? like memory and cost?
[00:02:43] Sofia: depends on model size and quantization. for a 13B open model, a preloaded instance might be ~30–40% of a full serving node cost if it's in a low-power standby mode — that's a rough. for 70B sizes it's higher. we'll provide region-specific cost estimates in the spreadsheet.
[00:02:58] [00:03:00] Liam: Can I jump in — important nuance is KV priming. if you do warm pool without KV priming you'll still pay a lot in first-request latency because K-V cache needs conversational prefixes. our KV warmup script replays representative prefixes from recent traffic (obfuscated) to populate KV shards.
[00:03:20] Rajiv: that replay sounds risky for PHI data — how do we ensure no sensitive tokens are stored or replayed?
[00:03:27] Sofia: good call. our recommended pattern is to use synthetic prompt templates derived from shape, not content. plus we scrub any PII and use synthetic IDs. we can also run warmup in a local-only mode inside your VPC so nothing leaves the network.
[00:03:42] Hannah: that local-only mode is a requirement for us. can you detail the peering workflow?
[00:03:46] Priya: sure. for VPC peering we support private endpoint backhaul. Redwood's private control plane negotiates via customer-provided peering and we expose an ingress endpoint inside your VPC. traffic stays in the peering path; logs are pushed to your S3 or GCS. we also support on-prem air-gapped installers if needed.
[00:04:04] Claire: do you need route-level NAT or specific inbound CIDR ranges?
[00:04:08] Priya: we ask for CIDR allowlist for the ingress endpoints and optional egress rules if you want to restrict outbound telemetry. we'll put a sample Terraform snippet in the repo.
[00:04:18] Marco: back to failover — what's the recommended order? do we fail to dedicated alternate region, then quantize, then degrade model?
[00:04:27] Sofia: recommended fallback chain is: 1) prefer alternate region with same model variant (if allowed by policy/residency), 2) if capacity constrained across all regions, switch to quantized variant (e.g., int8 or 4-bit variant) in-region or in alternate region, 3) if still overloaded, throttle non-essential endpoints or use low-cost streaming tokens, 4) last resort: synthetic fallback (short answer generated from cached responses) with explicit user-facing degraded notice.
[00:04:50] Jamal: can the switch to quantized happen per-request or is it per-instance rollout?
[00:04:54] Sofia: we can do per-request model selection at the proxy — the proxy can choose a compatible quantized runtime if the main path is at capacity, but that requires the quantized variant to be registered and warmed. otherwise it's a per-instance rollout.
[00:05:06] [00:05:20] Rajiv: latency impact of quantized fallback — any rough numbers?
[00:05:24] Sofia: quantized int8 often reduces memory and improves throughput; latency can be slightly lower per token, but you might see minor accuracy/regression cost. for our benchmarks, 1–2% degradation in output quality for high-quality quant; but it varies by workload. we'll attach eval metrics.
[00:05:38] Claire: another ops question — how is KV cache eviction coordinated across regions once failover happens? inconsistent K-V shards could cause hallucination or token mismatch.
[00:05:47] Sofia: important point. we don't replicate active KV shards globally by default because of size and consistency. our pattern is sticky session affinity coupled with prefix-level fallback. when we move a session cross-region, we can either: a) rehydrate KV by replaying a short suffix of the user's conversation (fast), b) accept a cold KV and route the next several tokens with reduced performance, or c) use a shared ephemeral cache layer (Redis/managed) which we can replicate asynchronously. each has tradeoffs.
[00:06:12] Hannah: replaying conversation — again compliance, we need to ensure the replay doesn't go to an external service. local-only replay inside VPC is necessary.
[00:06:20] Sofia: yep we support local-only warmup + streaming replay inside the peered VPC.
[00:06:25] [00:06:30] Liam: practical ops note — we recommend a warmup window of 3–5 minutes for typical session histories (2–3 turns) and 10–15 minutes for longer context. warmup time is a function of average turn length and kv shard size.
[00:06:45] Rajiv: our average session is long — 30 turns sometimes. 10–15 minutes warmup is tough for UX.
[00:06:51] Sofia: then we should consider sticky routing more aggressively with gradual reroute and only move sessions older than N minutes. also consider storing compacted context summaries in a global store to speed rehydration.
[00:07:05] Marco: compacted summaries could be PHI-sensitive. would need encryption and KMS in our VPC. thoughts?
[00:07:10] Priya: no problem — we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. any stored summaries can be encrypted with your key and never leave your network unencrypted. we also provide audit logs showing KMS usage.
[00:07:21] [00:07:30] Claire: can Redwood's routing plane call into our internal evaluation service to decide per-request policy? we have business rules that look up patient consent flags.
[00:07:38] Sofia: yes, we have a policy hook where the edge proxy queries a policy decision point (PDP) via low-latency call. we can cache decisions for short TTLs to avoid extra latency. you'll need to expose that PDP endpoint in peering.
[00:07:53] Jamal: latency budget — what is the extra hop cost for policy-checking and KV warmup?
[00:07:59] Sofia: PDP check typically adds 5–15ms if local; KV warmup cost is mainly initial token generation and cache fill — could add 200–800ms depending on number of prefixes. but warmup is asynchronous for the most part; first user facing request might see additional latency.
[00:08:18] [00:08:30] Evan: ok let's run a short scenario — europe primary region has a sudden CPU host failure and loses 40% capacity. what happens if queue depth climbs to 90%?
[00:08:41] Sofia: with the default policy (hard threshold at 85%), new sessions will start to be steered to us-east unless residency tag blocks it. existing sticky sessions will be honored for T minutes (configurable) then drained. we recommend a drain timeout of 2 minutes for short-lived sessions and up to 10 for longer conversations.
[00:09:00] Marco: draining can cause user-facing timeouts — what are rollback options?
[00:09:04] Liam: we support graceful degradation: fall back to a quantized variant for in-region sessions then slowly shift traffic. that keeps sessions local with slightly reduced quality rather than cross-region move which may have rehydration costs.
[00:09:17] Rajiv: i want the sequence recorded in a DR runbook with exact thresholds and who to call. can you sketch that now?
[00:09:23] Sofia: yeah quick sketch:
- Alert: region > 85% committed capacity for > 30s triggers P0 alert to SRE pager.
- Auto-response: proxy shifts 20% of new sessions per 30s to alternate region.
- If region stays > 90% for > 5m, escalate to hard-failover: shift 60–80% new sessions, enable quantized variant for remaining local sessions.
- Manual ops: runbook step to warm additional standby nodes (runbook link), notify security/team, coordinate KMS access if rehydration needed.
[00:09:58] [00:10:10] Claire: in the manual ops step, where does the KV warmup script run — in our VPC or Redwood side?
[00:10:16] Sofia: we support both. recommended for your compliance posture: run KV warmup inside your VPC against the private ingress endpoints. Redwood will provide the script and sample synthetic corpus.
[00:10:26] Hannah: sample corpus must be sanitized — we need a review step.
[00:10:29] Sofia: yes we'll provide an obfuscation step in the script and the output is dry-runable.
[00:10:33] [00:10:45] Evan: let's talk telemetry and debugging — when a session is moved, how do you trace which prefix was lost and what KV shard was rehydrated?
[00:10:53] Liam: we attach a session trace id to each request and keep a token-level map in the session store for N tokens. when a move happens we log a rehydration trace with the reason code, source shard id, and warmup replay steps. logs pushed to customer SIEM.
[00:11:11] Rajiv: we use Splunk — can you format logs to our ingestion pipeline?
[00:11:15] Liam: yes we ship JSON lines and can add the Splunk HEC token in the peered path.
[00:11:20] [00:11:30] Marco: in some of the Redwood docs i saw mention of 'continuous batching' — if we move sessions or quantize variants, does that break batching efficiency?
[00:11:39] Sofia: it can. continuous batching groups compatible requests; switching model variants or moving cross-region reduces batch hit-rate. to mitigate we maintain variant-aware batching queues and can do lightweight model-compatibility fallbacks so that quantized variants accept the same input shapes to maximize batching.
[00:11:57] Claire: what about memory pressure on GPU? in a failover we might spin up many instances and hit host OOMs if not careful.
[00:12:04] Sofia: our runtime does dynamic kernel selection and memory reservation — we can set per-instance memory headroom flags so the autoscaler respects safe headroom. also we recommend a warm-headroom buffer in the warm pool sizing.
[00:12:15] [00:12:30] Rajiv: would you recommend using a shared Redis for KV shards across regions to avoid rehydration costs? pros/cons?
[00:12:38] Sofia: pros — faster cross-region rehydration, consistent prefixes; cons — latency for remote Redis calls unless you deploy a geo-replicated managed redis (adds cost) and you need to manage encryption and keys. for PHI workloads we often recommend local-only KV and use compacted summaries or sticky routing to avoid remote calls.
[00:12:55] Hannah: from a security standpoint shared redis increases attack surface and must be restricted.
[00:12:59] Priya: you could also use a hybrid approach: critical prefixes stored locally, less-sensitive short-term context stored in a replicated store.
[00:13:09] [00:13:30] Sofia: moving on — quantization fallbacks and quality gating. we support automatic eval gating: when you enable a quantized variant we run real-time lightweight evals on a small holdout prompt set. if regression above threshold we can disable auto-fallback.
[00:13:46] Marco: who manages the holdout set? can we provide our own prompts?
[00:13:50] Sofia: yes you provide prompts and thresholds; Redwood also ships a default eval set. we'll surface the eval results in Console.
[00:13:59] Rajiv: curious about token accounting when switching models — if you move to quantized variant, are token counts and billing affected?
[00:14:06] Evan: billing is tied to the model variant; quantized variants may have a different per-token cost. we'll include cost delta in the spreadsheet.
[00:14:12] [00:14:30] Claire: let's do a brief demo — Sofia, can you show the proxy policy UI and a simulated failover?
[00:14:37] Sofia: yeah i'll share my screen. (screen sharing) ok on the policy editor you can define route-level residency tags, weightings, and thresholds. here's an example rule: europe-primary -> prefer-local, fallback-policy: gradual-shift 20%/30s, max-cross-region 60%.
[00:14:58] [00:15:10] Sofia: (demo continues) i'll flip the threshold to 80% to simulate — you can see the live metrics stream drop a marker and the route starts sending 20% of new sessions to us-east. logs show session_id, session_age, and why it moved.
[00:15:27] Claire: nice. can you simulate quantized fallback?
[00:15:30] Sofia: enabling quantized fallback now — policy toggle on screen — you'll see a flag 'quant_fallback: enabled', and a note that the quantized variant must be warm.
[00:15:40] [00:16:00] Sofia: ok switching to the KV warmup demo — i'll run a short synthetic replay that mimics a 3-turn conversation. (runs script) logs: warmup started, shards addressed: s-12, s-13; prefixes loaded: 42; estimated warmup latency 2.1s for first token.
[00:16:14] Rajiv: I see the logs but what's the mechanism to scrub content?
[00:16:18] Sofia: the script uses pattern-based scrubbers and a token frequency filter. we also provide a GDPR/PHI review tool that flags possible leaks.
[00:16:29] Marco: can we get the demo artifacts?
[00:16:31] Sofia: yes — i'll drop links after the call. (link: https://redwoodinference.com/internal/kv-warmup-demo — internal link placeholder)
[00:16:38] [00:17:00] Evan: okay shifting to runbook specifics — Liam can you walk through the manual steps if auto-failover doesn't stabilize?
[00:17:08] Liam: sure. manual runbook snippet:
1) Confirm alert and collect region metrics (p99, queue depth, node health).
2) If capacity < critical threshold, initiate warmup: run KV warmup in VPC, scale warm pool to N instances (commands included), and enable quantized variant for incoming sessions.
3) If still degraded after 10 minutes, open cross-region peering (if allowed) and move non-PHI traffic.
4) Traceroute affected session ids for debug, collect heapdumps if necessary, and contact Redwood SE for kernel-level debugging.
[00:17:42] Rajiv: who does step 3 on our side?
[00:17:45] Marco: platform team plus security sign-off.
[00:17:48] Liam: we'll include a checklist with exact CLI commands and expected log lines.
[00:17:54] [00:18:10] Claire: about autoscaling — will Redwood autoscaler respect our resource quotas inside peered VPC? we don't want Redwood to spin up thousands of nodes into our peering link.
[00:18:20] Priya: the autoscaler uses customer-provided quota caps and rate limits on scale-up. you set max instances per region for the private pool, and Redwood will never exceed that. we also support surge-protection policies.
[00:18:31] Hannah: plus we need audit trail for any scale decisions.
[00:18:34] Liam: all scale decisions are audited and pushed to your logs with decision_reason.
[00:18:38] [00:18:52] Evan: time check — we've got about an hour left; let's get into a couple of edge cases — on-prem cluster loses peering to the cloud but still has some compute, can it serve degraded traffic?
[00:18:58] Sofia: yes if the on-prem cluster has models loaded and kv shards present it can continue serving locally. the main problem is model version parity — you'll want a lighter quantized copy on-prem for DR so you can continue.
[00:19:10] Marco: how big is that quantized copy typically?
[00:19:13] Sofia: depends — 4-bit or int8 13B might be 10–15GB versus 30–40GB for FP16. so feasible for small on-prem hardware.
[00:19:20] [00:19:30] Rajiv: can we do cross-compile so the on-prem device uses a different kernel set? we have older GPUs.
[00:19:35] Sofia: our runtime has a kernel-selection layer; we can compile for older cuda versions but some older GPUs might need CPU offload or slower kernels. we'll test on your hardware matrix.
[00:19:46] Claire: testing matrix — we'll provide a list of host types.
[00:19:49] Evan: good. quick note on observability — in Console we'll provide per-route latency, per-model token breakdown, and kv-hit rate metric. these help tune where to set thresholds.
[00:20:02] [00:20:20] Marco: ok this is great. i want to raise one more concern — cost. if we aggressively keep warm pools in every region, cost explodes. any suggestions?
[00:20:30] Sofia: two levers: reduce warm pool size and rely on fast-notch scale up with warmup, or use predictive warmup based on expected traffic windows. Redwood Optimize can analyze your traffic and recommend warm pool schedules to minimize cost while meeting SLOs.
[00:20:46] Rajiv: predictive warmup sounds useful. does it integrate with our calendar/marketing events?
[00:20:50] Evan: yep you can provide event calendar hooks or integrate with your analytics to trigger warmup windows.
[00:20:55] [00:21:20] Jamal: we use some bursty workflows with hourly spikes — predictive warmup may work.
[00:21:26] Sofia: also consider mixed model strategy — keep a small warm pool of quantized instances always-on and only spin full-precision instances when necessary.
[00:21:36] Marco: let's talk about SLA — if we use dedicated capacity and still run into a failover event, what's Redwood's SLO for failover time?
[00:21:42] Evan: for Dedicated we commit to 99.9% regional availability and have documented failover RTO targets. Typical auto-failover to an alternate region can start within 60–120s depending on warm pool availability. full rehydration varies. we'll include exact SLA wording in the contract.
[00:21:58] [00:22:20] Hannah: any penetration testing considerations when the proxy consults external PDP or when we run warmup scripts?
[00:22:27] Priya: warmup scripts can be run in audit mode and are white-box friendly. the proxy-PDP calls use mTLS with mutual certs in the peered VPC; we support scanning and pentest coordination.
[00:22:38] Rajiv: cool. last technical nit — how do you handle model-specific tokens and tokenizer version skew across regions? we saw mismatch issues before.
[00:22:46] Sofia: we version tokenizers with model bundle and store tokenizer hash in session metadata. cross-region checks compare tokenizer hash before rehydration; if mismatch we either re-tokenize or fall back to compacted summary. the session trace will show tokenizer mismatch.
[00:23:01] [00:23:20] Evan: ok let's move to wrap — recap of decisions and next steps. Rajiv, Marco, Claire any immediate blockers?
[00:23:28] Marco: no blockers — need the spreadsheet and the warmup script and we'll validate on-prem hardware.
[00:23:34] Rajiv: security wants the obfuscation review and the peering Terraform snippet.
[00:23:38] Hannah: yes please, plus sample KMS policy.
[00:23:41] Evan: great. recap: Redwood to share region-capacity spreadsheet (cost+SLA), KV warmup script (sanitization enabled), runbook snippet + CLI commands, and a proposed DR tabletop window.
[00:23:54] Sofia: i'll attach demo artifacts and the sample policy file (link placeholder: https://redwoodinference.com/internal/policies).
[00:24:01] [00:24:30] Action item quick read: Evan sends spreadsheet; Sofia uploads scripts; Liam drafts runbook snippet; Rajiv shares routing table.
[00:24:45] Marco: thanks all. any final questions?
[00:24:50] Jamal: one last quick one — for logs retention, what default retention do you propose?
[00:24:55] Liam: default is 30 days, enterprise can extend to 1 year as an add-on.
[00:25:03] Claire: that's fine for now.
[00:25:10] Evan: awesome. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with threads.
